title: Accord with Conditions, Guard and Nurture
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: The original text is from the Theory of the Universal Essence of All Things.

inline.s: The original text is from the Theory of the Universal Essence of All Things.
All forms whatsoever are false and unreal; do not cling to forms, and abide unmoved in suchness.
The

Theory of the Universal Essence of All Things — an epoch-making Buddhist masterpiece that gathers what has come before and opens the way for what follows, an outline for the teaching of a whole age, a torch for the world of the Dharma’s decline. Compiled by the White-robed Layman Dingxi of Jinling after reading through all the scriptures, it may well be called “A New Treatise on Arousing Faith in the Mahayana.”

It is named the Theory of the Universal Essence of All Things because, since ancient times, Eastern and Western philosophy have alike been earnestly seeking the essence of the universe and of all things. This book therefore reveals to the world that Śākyamuni Buddha gave the correct answer more than two thousand years ago:
the essence of the universe and of all things is the reality of all dharmas, and the universe is a dream of ignorance; and it reveals how to wake from this dream.
(See the
Reality of All Dharmas
article.) Looking at modern science, the Buddha’s pronouncements are being confirmed one by one, all the more revealing the Buddha’s great wisdom, consummate and complete.

Because the author of this book concealed his name, his life story cannot be known; we can only judge the man by his writings: he was a layman of Jinling (Nanjing), a contemporary of Master Yinguang or slightly later. The layman’s style name was Dingxi. Dingxi is a homophone of “ding xi” — “certain to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.” The Master not only had a thorough mastery of Buddhist doctrine, with learning spanning both Chinese and Western traditions, but his own attainment in practice was also extremely high, with equal mastery of Chan and the Pure Land and boundless compassion — truly a great bodhisattva.

[Guard and nurture] Protection and spontaneous unfolding — these are the two stages of purifying habitual tendencies after seeing the nature. “Protection” means striving to tend the Holy Embryo so that it is not harmed by greed, anger, and delusion, thereby accomplishing the first two of the four patiences (the patience of subduing and the patience of gentle compliance); “spontaneous unfolding” means that, once the Holy Embryo has matured, it operates of itself, according with both favorable and adverse conditions, further refining it in the midst of them, so as to accomplish the latter two of the four patiences (the patience of non-arising and the patience of serene extinction). [Four patiences] The patience of subduing, the patience of gentle compliance, the patience of non-arising, and the patience of serene extinction. The patience of subduing: a beginner in practice who wishes to endure adverse and favorable conditions (free from greed, anger, and delusion) must first bring his mind into submission. The patience of gentle compliance: after the mind has long been brought into submission, when encountering objects and conditions one can endure naturally, without forced suppression (free of greed, anger, and delusion); at this point the mind is gentle and compliant. The patience of non-arising: one who is in the stage of sagehood realizes that all dharmas originally neither arise; sentient and insentient alike arise from conditions and lack self-nature, empty in their very substance. Therefore, within the nature that lacks self-nature, the mind of patience is unmoved, directly realizing non-arising. The patience of serene extinction: one at the stage of fruition thoroughly realizes the realm of nirvāṇic serene extinction; the two characteristics of motion and stillness both accord with suchness. [Suchness] The realm of self-nature, free from inverted discrimination. Because it is the true suchness (the reality of all dharmas) realized by wisdom that accords with reality, it is called “suchness.”
Note:
The sub-headings in this article were added by the annotator.

[From ages past to the present, all things and events arise only from causes and conditions, and are transformed only by the mind-consciousness. Like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning, they are ultimately empty in substance, with no self-nature. Person and dharmas suddenly become still, all conditions come to rest of themselves; facing objects, one accords with conditions, passing through without leaving a trace.]

All things and events, from ages past to the present, arise only from causes and conditions, and are transformed only by the mind-consciousness. They are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, like a spark from flint or a flash of lightning — ultimately empty in substance, with no self-nature. Having realized this truth, attachment to a self and attachment to dharmas suddenly become still, and all conditions come to rest of themselves; facing objects, one accords with everything, passing through without leaving a trace (afterwards one does not dwell on it, like a picture drawn on water, vanishing as soon as it is drawn).
[Ultimately empty in substance] All dharmas are illusions, without a real substance. (See the
Reality of All Dharmas

article.) [Twofold emptiness of person and dharma] Emptiness of person and emptiness of dharma. Also called the emptiness of self and dharmas. No attachment to a self, because the body and mind are a false union of the five aggregates, with no real, permanent, unified, sovereign self-entity — this is called emptiness of person. No attachment to dharmas, because all dharmas are illusory, with no real substance — this is called emptiness of dharma. [Sudden stillness of person and dharmas] Attachment to a self and attachment to dharmas suddenly become extinct. [Flint-spark and lightning] A description of all things and events that, like lightning and a spark from flint, vanish in an instant. [No self-nature] Without a nature of one’s own. This means all dharmas have no real substance and are illusions. It is also called the absence of a nature. The Lotus Sutra says:
“Know that all dharmas always have no nature.”
The Surangama Sutra says:
“All illusions become without nature.”

[Always keep the mind empty and bright, clear and transparent, like a mirror reflecting objects, responding to conditions and reflecting them. Coming, it is not anticipated; departing, there is no lingering; it is not deluded by objects, and is attached to nothing. It does not approach a dharma, does not leave a dharma, does not dwell in a dharma, does not think of a dharma, does not see a dharma, does not obstruct a dharma. It neither grasps nor rejects, neither craves nor is dull, neither stalls nor clings, neither follows nor destroys. It neither establishes nor accepts, neither moves nor expels, neither self nor other, neither drowsy nor scattered.]

Always keep the mind empty and bright, clear and transparent, like a mirror reflecting objects, responding to conditions and reflecting them. Coming, it is not anticipated; departing, there is no lingering; it is not deluded by objects, and is attached to nothing. It neither approaches (does not cling to) a dharma, nor leaves a dharma, nor dwells in a dharma, nor thinks of a dharma, nor sees a dharma, nor obstructs a dharma. It neither grasps nor rejects, neither craves nor is dull, neither stalls nor clings, neither follows nor destroys (neither follows it nor denies it). It neither establishes nor accepts (does not show favor or disfavor, nor is it influenced by it), neither moves nor expels (it is not moved by it, nor does it drive it away), neither self nor other, neither drowsy nor scattered.
[Like a mirror reflecting objects] Though the mirror reflects objects and responds to conditions, the mirror and the objects it reflects are mutually unrelated.

[Only let the six consciousnesses issue from the six gates, and amid the six sense-objects be undefiled and unmixed. Thought after thought dwelling in truth, yet utterly ungraspable; thought after thought perfect and bright, originally pure and spontaneous. Do not practice contemplative exercise, nor still the mind; do not be bound by dharmas, nor turned by objects. Sweep freely in every direction, roaming at ease with conditions; at all times and in all places, be without mind and without contrivance.]

Only let the six consciousnesses issue from the six gates, and amid the six sense-objects be undefiled and unmixed. Thought after thought dwelling in truth, and the ten thousand dharmas are utterly ungraspable; thought after thought perfect and bright, and the self-nature is originally pure and spontaneous. Do not practice contemplative exercise, nor still the mind; do not be bound by dharmas, nor turned by objects. Sweep freely in every direction, roaming at ease with conditions; at all times and in all places, be without mind and without contrivance.

[Six gates] That is, the six sense-roots: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. [Six consciousnesses] Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. These are the discriminating functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, feeling, and thinking, which arise from the six sense-roots (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) meeting the six sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas). [Contemplative exercise] Contemplating principle in the mind and practicing the body in accord with principle. [Roaming at ease] Free and unconverted, unconstrained.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“Just purify the original mind, so that the six consciousnesses issue from the six gates, and amid the six sense-objects are undefiled and unmixed, coming and going freely, universally applied without obstruction — this is the samādhi of prajñā, sovereign and liberated, called the practice of no-thought.”
The Compendium of the Five Lamps records that the Fourth Patriarch of Chan, Daoxin, instructed Farong, saying:
“The hundreds and thousands of Dharma-gates all return to the square inch
(the mind)

; the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all lie in the source of the mind. All the precepts-gate, concentration-gate, wisdom-gate, and spiritual powers and transformations are fully complete within you and are not apart from your mind. All afflictions and karmic hindrances are originally empty and still; all causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world to escape, and no bodhi to seek. Humans and non-humans, nature and characteristics, are equal. The great Way is [empty
(vacant)
] and vast, cutting off thought and deliberation. Such a Dharma as this you have now attained, and there is no lack
(deficiency)

; how are you different from a Buddha? There is no other Dharma. Only let your mind be free and at ease; do not practice contemplative exercise, nor still the mind; do not arouse greed or anger, nor harbor worry or anxiety; be free and unobstructed, sweeping freely in every direction. Do no good, and do no evil. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, whatever meets the eye, whatever conditions are encountered, all are the wondrous functioning of the Buddha — happy and free of worry — therefore it is called being a Buddha.”
[Farong (

)] The founder of the Niutou school. [Source of the mind] Since the mind is the root-source of all dharmas, it is called the source of the mind. The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says: “If the deluded mind arises, know it and do not follow it. When delusion ceases, the source of the mind is empty and still; all virtues are complete, and its wondrous functions are inexhaustible.” The Cessation and Contemplation says: “Sitting cross-legged with hands folded, sealing the lips and closing the tongue, contemplating reality — the source of the mind being one-pointed, the whole realm of dharmas is likewise still.” It also says: “If you wish to know clearly, you must know the source of the mind. As the source of the mind is not two, then all dharmas are all the same as empty space.” [Non-humans] Refers to the non-human beings — the eight classes of dragons and deities, as well as yakshas, evil ghosts, asuras, hell-beings, and so on. Generally it is also used as a general term for ghosts and spirits. [Self-mastery] When the mind is free from the bondage of afflictions, and has reached through without obstruction, it is called self-mastery. The Lotus Sutra

chapter “Sequential Teachings,” says: “Having ended all the fetters of existence, the mind attains self-mastery.” [Fetters of existence] “Existence” refers to the retribution of birth-and-death; “fetters” refers to the afflictions that can draw forth this retribution. Greed, anger, delusion, and the other afflictions can bind a person and keep him dwelling in the realm of birth-and-death, unable to escape; hence they are called the fetters of existence.

[Motion and stillness in suchness, the nature ever self-mastered. Well it illuminates all illusions, like a mirror without a trace. It discriminates all dharmas, yet attains non-arising. It follows all conditions, with no obstruction and no hindrance. The ground of the mind is open and free, unfolding spontaneously. Like a fool, a mind like a rock, caring not whether the people of the world know it or not. It applies all the sense-roots, yet is undefiled by all objects. Birth-and-death dharmas pass through the mind and do not enter.]

Motion and stillness in suchness, the self-nature ever self-mastered. Well it illuminates all illusions, like a mirror reflecting objects — the object departs and the mirror is empty, leaving no trace. Well it discriminates all dharmas, yet without clinging to forms, abiding unmoved in suchness. It follows all conditions, with neither obstruction nor hindrance. The ground of the mind is broad and free, unfolding spontaneously. Like a fool, the mind like a rock, caring not whether the people of the world know it or not. It applies all the sense-roots, yet is undefiled by all objects. Birth-and-death dharmas pass through the mind and do not dwell within it.

[Suchness] The realm of self-nature, free from inverted discrimination. Because it is the true suchness (the reality of all dharmas) realized by wisdom that accords with reality, it is called “suchness.” [Spontaneous unfolding] According with conditions and operating naturally. [Unfolding] Ceaselessly surging and rolling. [Birth-and-death dharmas pass through the mind and do not enter] Birth-and-death dharmas pass through the mind and do not enter into it. For example, when an annoying mechanical noise from outside the window arises, you can imagine your own body and mind transparent and unobstructed, letting the noise pass straight through without reacting.

[Like empty space, containing within it all kinds of forms, yet making no discrimination among these various realms. The true nature abides forever, bright and numinous, clearly known of itself; one attains the original wondrous mind. Silencing the mind to merge with the Way, practice and understanding answering each other, guarding it diligently in secret — this is called guarding.]

Like empty space, containing within it the myriad forms of the universe, yet making no discrimination among these various realms. The true nature abides forever, bright and numinous, clearly known of itself; one attains the original wondrous mind. Silencing the mind to merge with the Way, practice and understanding answering each other, guarding it diligently in secret — this is called guarding.
[Silencing the mind to merge with the Way] Extinguishing the thoughts of the mind, and merging with the great Way.

[Sitting quietly by the water’s edge, deep within the forest of the mountains, nourishing the Holy Embryo, cultivating the naga concentration. Entering emptiness from the provisional, contemplate all dharmas: the self-nature does not arise, the Dharma-nature abides forever. Realize non-arising in one’s own body, sever all idle talk, extinguish the cause of birth-and-death, and from the true emerge into the mundane.]

Sitting quietly by the water’s edge, deep within the forest of the mountains, nourishing the Holy Embryo, cultivating the naga concentration. Entering emptiness from the provisional, gathering the forms back into the nature, contemplate all dharmas: the self-nature does not arise, the Dharma-nature abides forever. Realize non-arising in one’s own body, sever all idle talk, extinguish the cause of birth-and-death, and, following the truth, go beyond the mundane.

[Holy Embryo] The three stages of worthy beings among the stages of bodhisattva practice — the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications — are called the “Holy Embryo,” because through cultivating the true Dharma they are nourished and grown, until reaching the first ground and seeing the Way, and are born into the Buddha’s family. [Fifty-two stages] From an ordinary person to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages in all: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, the grade of equal enlightenment, and the grade of wondrous enlightenment. [First ground] The first of the ten grounds. [Naga concentration] “Naga” is translated as “dragon.” The “naga concentration” is the “dragon concentration,” like a dragon lurking in the deep abyss. [Two truths] The mundane truth and the true truth. The mundane truth, also called the worldly truth or the conventional truth, is the mundane phenomena seen by ordinary beings; the true truth, also called the supreme truth or the ultimate truth, is the true principle seen by sagely wisdom — that is, the internally-realized Dharma-nature that is beyond words.
[Inner realization and outer guidance] Within, realize the true, so as to escape birth-and-death; without, guide the ten thousand practices, so as to enter the ocean of vows.

[Contemplate all dharmas: they arise from the union of causes and conditions, and the effects of karma are not lost. With compassion and benefit, gather in and transform sentient beings, removing their pain and giving them joy. Within, realize the true, so as to escape birth-and-death; without, guide the ten thousand practices, so as to enter the ocean of vows. For all future ages, with the power of wisdom, accord with sentient beings, causing them to arouse bodhi, to gain the deep benefit of the Dharma, and all of them to attain liberation. This utmost compassion, this ultimate great kindness, is accomplished by the prajñā wisdom of emptiness.]

Contemplate all dharmas: they all arise from the union of causes and conditions, and the effects of karma are not lost. With compassion and benefit, gather in and transform sentient beings, removing their pain and giving them joy. Within, realize the true, so as to escape birth-and-death; without, guide the ten thousand practices, so as to enter the ocean of vows. For all future ages, with the power of wisdom, accord with sentient beings, causing them to arouse the bodhi mind, to gain the deep benefit of the Dharma, and all of them to attain liberation. Such utmost compassion, such ultimate great kindness, is accomplished by the prajñā wisdom of emptiness.

[Benefit] To cause people to receive benefit. [Ocean of vows] The bodhisattva’s vows are both deep and vast, like the boundless ocean. The Avatamsaka Sutra says: “Ever using the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows that has been attained, cause all sentient beings to be complete in the wisdom-body.”

blocks.text: 8. The Dual Practice of Compassion and Wisdom

inline.s: [Dwelling apart from wrong views, not abiding in birth-and-death; arousing great compassion, not abiding in nirvāṇa. Awakening oneself and awakening others, the dual practice of compassion and wisdom, practicing the Tathagata’s practice, entering the Buddha’s realm. Wisdom and skillful means, understanding the world as illusory, provisionally manifesting in the world, in limitless illusory dharmas.]

Dwelling apart from wrong views, not abiding in birth-and-death; arousing great compassion, not abiding in nirvāṇa. Awakening oneself and awakening others, the dual practice of compassion and wisdom, practicing the Tathagata’s practice, entering the Buddha’s realm. Wisdom realizes the substance (realizes the reality of dharmas) while provisionally practicing skillful means; though one understands that worldly affairs are illusory, one still responds to the occasion and manifests the limitless illusory dharmas of the world to transform sentient beings.

[Not abiding in nirvāṇa] Because of great compassion, the bodhisattva pities sentient beings, and therefore does not abide in nirvāṇa but transforms them. [Awakening oneself and awakening others] Awakening oneself, and also causing others to awaken.

[Skillful means not abandoned: relying on all wisdom, yet manifesting in the world the realm of ignorance. Skillful means not abandoned: going beyond the world, yet manifesting in the world the realm of defilement. Skillful means not abandoned: the bodhisattva’s reality, yet manifesting while dwelling in the world the realm of ordinary beings. Skillful means not abandoned: the true of non-arising, yet manifesting in the world the realm of illusions. Skillful means not abandoned: the purity of nirvāṇa, yet manifesting in the world the realm of clamor. Skillful means not abandoned: profound meditative concentration, yet manifesting in the world the realm of turmoil. Skillful means not abandoned: the single characteristic of equality, yet manifesting in the world the realm of differences.]

Skillful means not abandoned: relying on all wisdom, yet manifesting in the world the realm of ignorance. Skillful means not abandoned: going beyond the world, yet manifesting in the world the realm of defilement. Skillful means not abandoned: relying on the bodhisattva’s reality, yet manifesting while dwelling in the world the realm of ordinary beings. Skillful means not abandoned: relying on the true of non-arising, yet manifesting in the world the realm of illusions. Skillful means not abandoned: relying on the purity of nirvāṇa, yet manifesting in the world the realm of clamor. Skillful means not abandoned: relying on profound meditative concentration, yet manifesting in the world the realm of turmoil. Skillful means not abandoned: relying on the single characteristic of equality, yet manifesting in the world the realm of differences.

[Skillful means not abandoned] The bodhisattva, practicing compassion and wisdom together, relies on the true truth to exercise skillful means, without abandoning the mundane truth. [Skillful means] Means, methods, or language adopted in accord with the occasion to guide and transform sentient beings.
[Encountering things, all is true] Within manifest birth-and-death, one sees only non-arising.

[All the realms of the world, in their many kinds, are exactly the Tathagata’s realm of reality. There is no difference, no obstruction, no boundary, no measure. Seeing principle within things: things are principle, the provisional is the empty — they do not go beyond or cut off from each other. Green bamboos and yellow flowers are no other than prajñā; blue mountains and emerald waters are all true suchness. The wondrous nature of true suchness is not constrained by things; touch upon existence or non-existence, and you are separated by the distance of heaven and earth. The wise comprehend this, and encountering things all is true; the deluded do not comprehend, and the more they turn, the farther they go.]

Gathering the forms back into the nature, the many realms of the world are exactly the Tathagata’s realm of reality. There is no difference, no obstruction, no boundary, no measure. Seeing principle within things: things are principle; the provisional is the empty — they do not go beyond or cut off from each other. Green bamboos and yellow flowers are no other than prajñā; blue mountains and emerald waters are all true suchness. The wondrous nature of true suchness is not constrained by things; touch upon existence or non-existence, and you are separated by the distance of heaven and earth. The wise comprehend this: gathering the forms back into the nature, encountering things all is true; the deluded do not comprehend, and are turned by forms; the more they turn, the more they go, and the farther (from reality) they go.

[Measure] Without the discrimination of quantities (number, weight, degree, and so on). [Gathering the forms back into the nature] Dissolving the myriad forms of the universe back into the reality of all dharmas; within manifest birth-and-death, seeing only non-arising. (See the
Reality of All Dharmas
article.) [Heaven and earth] Heaven and earth. Often used to describe an extreme difference: a difference as between heaven and earth.

[Thought after thought merging with the Way, step after step seeing non-arising; the mind ever bright and still, applying with self-mastery. Following the nature, at ease and free, with no dwelling or clinging at all; whatever meets the eye, whatever conditions are encountered, all are wondrous functioning.]

Thought after thought merging with the Way, step after step seeing non-arising; the mind ever bright and still, applying with self-mastery, without obstruction. Following the nature, at ease and free, with no dwelling or clinging at all; whatever meets the eye, whatever conditions are encountered, all are wondrous functioning.

[The dharmas of the world are the very mark of nirvāṇa; every path is the Way, every dharma fully manifested. Answering the outflows-free, is called the outflows-free wisdom; this very body and mind, self-mastered and liberated. Mind after mind in serene extinction, the awakened nature fully manifested, naturally flowing into the wisdom of all modes.]

The dharmas of the world are the very mark of nirvāṇa; every matter (head by head) is the Way, every dharma (dharma by dharma) fully manifests the Way. Answering the outflows-free, is called the outflows-free wisdom; this very body and mind, self-mastered and liberated. Mind after mind in serene extinction, the awakened nature fully manifested, naturally flowing into the wisdom of all modes.

[Every path is the Way] This means the Way is nowhere absent. [Outflows-free] Pure, without afflictions. “Outflow” is another name for affliction. [Outflows-free wisdom] The pure wisdom apart from all afflictions; this wisdom has the function of severing delusion and realizing the true. [This very body and mind, self-mastered and liberated] Self-mastered and liberated right now, without waiting for the end of life. [Wisdom of all modes] The wisdom whereby the Buddha penetrates the common and the particular characteristics of all dharmas, and, in transforming beings, severs delusion. [Common characteristic] The characteristic common to all dharmas. [Particular characteristic] The characteristic peculiar to each dharma.
